bracket: [Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(\dfrac{2}{7}\), which is the JOINT probability \(P(R_1 \cap B_2) = \dfrac{3}{7} \times \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{7}\) — the chance that the first marble is red AND the second is blue. The question as printed states that the first marble drawn IS red, so it asks for the conditional probability, and with 2 red and 4 blue left in the bag that is \(\dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}\). The stem was checked word for word against the printed page; the key answers a question the stem does not ask.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(\dfrac{4}{5}\). With equal priors, \(P(A) = \tfrac12(0.2) + \tfrac12(0.3) = 0.25\) and \(P(E_1/A) = \dfrac{0.1}{0.25} = \dfrac{2}{5}\). The printed \(\dfrac{4}{5}\) is \(\dfrac{0.2}{0.25}\) — the prior \(\tfrac12\) was dropped from the numerator while retained in the denominator. Two independent checks: the posteriors must sum to 1, and \(\dfrac{2}{5} + \dfrac{3}{5} = 1\) whereas \(\dfrac{4}{5}\) does not; and since \(P(A/E_1) < P(A/E_2)\), observing \(A\) must pull \(E_1\) BELOW its prior of \(\tfrac12\), so no answer above \(\tfrac12\) is possible.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(\dfrac{3}{5}\) for BOTH sub-items. That is the correct answer to (ii) — Y's odds are given AGAINST, \(2 : 3\), so \(P(Y) = \dfrac{3}{5}\) — copied up into (i). X's odds are given IN FAVOUR, \(4 : 3\), so \(P(X) = \dfrac{4}{4+3} = \dfrac{4}{7}\). No reading of 'odds in favour \(4 : 3\)' produces \(\dfrac{3}{5}\).]

[Textbook misprint: the printed key lists \(A = \{RR, GR, RB, RP, GR, BR, PR\}\) — GR appears twice and RG is missing. The cardinality of 7 is right and the intended set is unambiguous, so this is a typographical slip in the key rather than a mathematical error; the correct set is \(\{RR, RG, RB, RP, GR, BR, PR\}\).]

[Textbook misprint: the printed key gives \(\dfrac{14}{19}\ (0.733)\). The fraction is correct but \(\dfrac{14}{19} = 0.7368\ldots\), i.e. \(0.737\) to three decimal places, not \(0.733\). The decimal gloss only is wrong.]

[Textbook misprint: the printed formula line shows the numerator as \(p(T/S)P(S)\) where it must be \(P(T'/S')P(S') = 0.90 \times 0.995 = 0.8955\) — which is the value the book itself then substitutes. Its denominator \(0.8958\) is \(1 - P(T) = 0.89575\) rounded. The printed final value is correct.]

[Textbook misprint: options B and C are printed identically as \(\dfrac{5}{8}\), so the question offers only three distinct alternatives. This does not move the key — the correct value \(\dfrac{5}{14}\) is option A and both members of the duplicated pair are distractors — but one alternative is a dead duplicate.]

[Textbook misprint: the stem never states HOW the book is chosen. Read literally — every book on both shelves equally likely — the answer is \(\dfrac{9}{14}\), which is also a printed option. The keyed answer \(\dfrac{31}{48}\) requires the reading that a SHELF is chosen at random and then a book from it, which is what makes the 8-versus-6 split relevant. The key's reading is followed here; a student who answers \(\dfrac{9}{14}\) has read the stem as printed.]

[Textbook misprint: the stem reads 'A fair is tossed twice' — the noun is missing. Its own later reference to 'the second die' identifies a die, which is how it is solved here. The arithmetic is unaffected.]

[Textbook misprint: the stem reads 'the odds in favour of solving the same problem are 7 to 5', naming no second solver, so as printed it gives two different odds for one event. The book's own parallel question (Exercise 9.5 Q.2) reads 'the odds in favour of Rafi solving the same problem', which identifies the dropped name. The printed key \(\dfrac{16}{21}\) confirms the two-solver reading — the one-solver reading cannot produce it.]

[Textbook misprint: the printed solution gives \(E_1 \cup E_4 = \{HTT, HTH, THH, HHH, HHT\}\), but HTT has only one head so it lies in neither \(E_1\) (at least 2 heads) nor \(E_4\) (exactly 2 heads); the union is \(\{HHH, HHT, HTH, THH\}\). The line printed \(E_3 = \{HHH, HHT, HTH, THH\}\) is really \(E_3'\) — contradicted by the book's own \(E_3 = \{HTT, THT, TTH, TTT\}\) two lines above.]

[Textbook misprint: the printed solution ends \(P(B) = \dfrac{6}{120} = \dfrac{1}{120}\). The working is correct (3! = 6 favourable arrangements out of 120), but \(\dfrac{6}{120} = \dfrac{1}{20}\), not \(\dfrac{1}{120}\).]

[Textbook misprint: the book names the event \(A\) and then refers to it twice as \(X\) ('X and Y are mutually exclusive events' and \(1 - P(X \cup Y)\)). The arithmetic that follows uses \(A\) and is correct.]

[Textbook misprint: the printed solution opens 'Since \(1 - P(A') = 0.7\)', contradicting both the given \(P(A') = 0.7\) and its own next line \(P(A) = 1 - P(A') = 1 - 0.7 = 0.3\). The leading \(1 -\) is spurious; the rest is correct.]

[Textbook misprint: the last line of the printed solution reads \(\left(\dfrac{48}{154}\right)\left(\dfrac{45}{154}\right) = \dfrac{93}{154}\) — the \(+\) between the two fractions is missing, so as printed it reads as a product. The stated answer \(\dfrac{93}{154}\) is correct and is their SUM.]
